full_text_en:
Jiang Haixin v. Philips Corporation — dispute over computer network domain name

[Ruling Summary]

According to Article 5 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Computer Network Domain Names, the registration and use of a domain name that is identical or similar to another person's registered trademark, without a justifiable reason for registration or use, and sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to be misled, shall be deemed as malicious registration and use of the domain name.

Plaintiff: Jiang Haixin, male, 30 years old, residing at No. 101, Huqingping Highway, Shanghai.

Defendant: Koninklijke Philips Electronics N.V. (Royal Philips Electronics of the Netherlands), domiciled at Groenewoudseweg, Eindhoven, The Netherlands.

The plaintiff, Jiang Haixin, filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court against the defendant, Koninklijke Philips Electronics N.V. (hereinafter referred to as Philips), over a dispute concerning a computer network domain name.

The plaintiff alleged: After the defendant's complaint, the Arbitration and Mediation Center of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) ruled that the domain name philipscis.com registered by the plaintiff should be transferred to the defendant. The plaintiff contended that: 1. The defendant's trademark consists of the seven letters "PHILIPS," while the domain name registered by the plaintiff is "philipscis.com," which adds three letters "cis" to the defendant's trademark. As for the added "cis" or "scis," if used as English abbreviations, they have broader meanings and are not identifiers of the defendant's Communication, Security & Imaging (CSI) division. The domain name registered by the plaintiff is neither identical nor similar to the defendant's trademark and will not cause confusion. The defendant cannot claim that all domain names containing the word "PHILIPS" should belong to it. 2. The domain name philipscis.com is composed of three parts: the common male English name "philip," and "sc" and "is." The plaintiff registered it as a domain name not only because "philip" is a common name but also because it has been the plaintiff's English name since youth; "sc" is the abbreviation for Shanghai, China, the plaintiff's place of residence; and "is" is the abbreviation for Internet System or Internet Server. These words have special meanings for the plaintiff. The plaintiff registered it as a domain name without any malicious intent. 3. Prior to the domain name dispute between the defendant and the plaintiff, the plaintiff had already used search engines such as Google.com and Yahoo.com to register the domain name philipscis.com, making it known to Internet users. On the website opened with this domain name, the plaintiff prominently displayed the dynamic Chinese and English logo of the company, indicating the website owner, which would not mislead Internet users. On this website, the plaintiff, authorized by a special distributor of Philips security and communication systems, sold only the defendant's communication, video, and security system products, technical support, and services to users. The plaintiff neither treated the defendant as a competitor nor interfered with the defendant's business operations, thus using the domain name reasonably and in good faith. 4. After the plaintiff launched the website with the domain name philipscis.com to a wide range of Internet users, the defendant initiated a domain name dispute through WIPO, demonstrating malicious intent to seize the plaintiff's domain name. 5. The WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center used a sole panelist to hear the domain name dispute initiated by the defendant. When Singapore citizen Leong Kah Wei, as an expert, heard a case from China, despite her familiarity with the Chinese language and script, there were inevitably differences in regional and cultural understanding and expression, as well as personal bias and other factors, leading to an unfair outcome. The plaintiff's registration and use of the domain name philipscis.com did not infringe the defendant's trademark rights, and the WIPO panel's decision was unfounded. Therefore, the plaintiff requested: 1. Revocation or suspension of the WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center's decision; 2. A judgment awarding the domain name philipscis.com to the plaintiff.

The defendant argued: Philips's PHILIPS trademark has been registered in the Netherlands since 1891 and subsequently in many countries around the world, including China. Philips has spent significant sums to maintain this trademark, making it one of the company's most important assets. The defendant contended: 1. The first seven letters of the disputed domain name are completely identical to the defendant's PHILIPS trademark, easily causing confusion. 2. The defendant never authorized the plaintiff to use the PHILIPS trademark or slogan on its website. The plaintiff ignored the defendant's letters requesting it to cease using the disputed domain name and continued to use it, and the plaintiff has not been generally recognized through this use, nor does it have any legal interest in this domain name. 3. The plaintiff not only used a domain name containing the PHILIPS trademark to open its own website but also copied the layout of the defendant's website homepage on that site, sold the defendant's "Communication and Video Security System" products, and promoted related services, even using the defendant's globally renowned service slogan "let's make things better" on its own website. The content of the plaintiff's other Chinese website, philipscss.com.cn, was identical to this website. Knowing that the PHILIPS trademark is a well-known mark, the plaintiff still registered and used a domain name containing PHILIPS in this manner, demonstrating clear malice. 4. The WIPO panel's hearing, both procedurally and substantively, complied with the provisions of relevant intellectual property treaties. In summary, the plaintiff's registration and use of the disputed domain name indeed infringed the defendant's trademark rights, and therefore the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed.

Upon trial, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts:

The defendant Philips's PHILIPS trademark has been registered in nearly 150 countries worldwide. In 1980, the PHILIPS trademark was registered in China under Registration No. 135046. "Let's make things better" is a promotional slogan used globally by Philips. Philips has a department called CSI (Communication, Security & Imaging), and the website corresponding to this department uses the domain name philipscsi.com.

The plaintiff, Jiang Haixin, is the legal representative of Shanghai Xinwu Intelligent System Engineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinwu Company). This company, authorized by a special distributor of Philips security and communication systems, is approved to engage in the design, installation, and maintenance of Philips communication, security, and video system products in mainland China. On March 1, 2002, Jiang Haixin registered the domain name philipscis.com and launched a corresponding English website using this domain name. On the homepage of this website printed on September 28, 2002, the words "Communication, Security & Imaging" were centered, a link titled "ABOUT PHILIPSCSI" was placed at the upper left, the words "let's make things better" were at the upper right, a "CSI NEWS" column was on the right, and the copyright owner was indicated as Xinwu Company at the bottom.

On September 19, 2002, the WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center issued a decision on the complaint filed by the applicant Philips (the defendant in this case), finding that: 1. The disputed domain name philipscis.com is completely or confusingly similar to the trademark (PHILIPS) in which the applicant has rights; 2. The respondent (the plaintiff in this case) has no rights or legitimate interests in the disputed domain name; 3. The respondent's registration and use of the disputed domain name were in bad faith. Accordingly, it ordered that the disputed domain name philipscis.com be transferred to the applicant. Dissatisfied with this decision, the plaintiff Jiang Haixin filed a lawsuit with the court. The domain name registrar has now suspended the execution of the WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center's decision.

The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court held that this case is a foreign-related civil dispute concerning infringement. Pursuant to Article 146(1) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the laws of China shall apply to this case.

This case involves trademark infringement and domain name registration and use. The relevant laws and judicial interpretations of China include: Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China provides that causing other damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark constitutes infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. Article 1(3) of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Trademark Civil Disputes provides that "registering a word that is identical or similar to another person's registered trademark as a domain name and using that domain name to conduct e-commerce in related goods, which is likely to cause relevant members of the public to be misled," constitutes "other damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark" under Article 52(5) of the Trademark Law. Article 4 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Computer Network Domain Names provides: "When trying a domain name dispute case, a people's court shall find that the defendant's registration and use of a domain name constitutes infringement or unfair competition if the following conditions are met: (1) The civil rights and interests that the plaintiff seeks to protect are legitimate and valid; (2) The defendant's domain name or its main part constitutes a reproduction, imitation, translation, or transliteration of the plaintiff's well-known trademark, or is identical or similar to the plaintiff's registered trademark, domain name, etc., sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to be misled; (3) The defendant has no rights or interests in the domain name or its main part, nor justifiable reasons for registering or using the domain name; (4) The defendant registered and used the domain name in bad faith." Article 5 provides: "If the defendant's conduct is proven to fall under any of the following circumstances, the people's court shall find that the defendant acted in bad faith: (1) Registering another person's well-known trademark as a domain name for commercial purposes; (2) Registering or using a domain name identical or similar to the plaintiff's registered trademark, domain name, etc., for commercial purposes, intentionally creating confusion with the goods, services, or website provided by the plaintiff, and misleading Internet users to access its website or other online sites; (3) Attempting to sell, rent, or otherwise transfer the domain name at a high price to obtain improper benefits; (4) After registering a domain name, not using it or preparing to use it, but intentionally preventing the right holder from registering the domain name; (5) Having other circumstances showing bad faith." "If the defendant proves that the domain name it held before the dispute had acquired certain visibility and could be distinguished from the plaintiff's registered trademark, domain name, etc., or there are other circumstances sufficient to show that it did not act in bad faith, the people's court may find that the defendant did not act in bad faith."

Based on the above laws and judicial interpretations, and in light of the disputes between the parties, the following issues need to be resolved in this case: 1. Is the defendant Philips's trademark protected by Chinese law? 2. Is the domain name registered and used by the plaintiff Jiang Haixin similar to Philips's trademark and sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to be misled? 3. Does Jiang Haixin have justifiable reasons for registering and using the domain name, and does he have rights or interests in the domain name or its main part? 4. Did Jiang Haixin act in bad faith in registering and using the domain name? Once these four issues are resolved, the focus of the dispute between the parties—to whom the disputed domain name belongs—will be clear.

Regarding the first issue: The defendant Philips's PHILIPS trademark has been registered in China, and Philips has legitimate and valid trademark rights in the PHILIPS trademark. Both parties have no dispute on this point, and the plaintiff Jiang Haixin even acknowledged that the PHILIPS trademark is a well-known mark.

Regarding the second issue: The first seven letters of the domain name philipscis.com registered by the plaintiff Jiang Haixin are completely identical to the defendant Philips's PHILIPS trademark, and the last three letters "cis" differ only in order from the abbreviation "CSI" of the defendant's department. Therefore, it should be found that this domain name is similar to Philips's trademark and is sufficient to cause relevant members of the public to be misled.

Regarding the third issue: 1. The plaintiff Jiang Haixin claimed that "philip" is his English name, "sc" is the abbreviation of his place of residence, and "is" is the abbreviation of Internet system or server. Jiang Haixin could not explain why he connected his English name and place of residence with the abbreviation of Internet system or server to register as a domain name. Therefore, Jiang Haixin's explanation is too far-fetched and unconvincing. 2. Jiang Haixin claimed that he was legally authorized by a special distributor of Philips security and communication systems to sell Philips communication, video, and security system products, and that the website was established for this sales activity, so there was nothing improper in registering and using this domain name. In fact, the entity authorized to sell Philips communication, video, and security system products was Xinwu Company, not Jiang Haixin. Moreover, trademarks and products have different rights; obtaining the right to distribute another person's products does not simultaneously give the right to use that person's trademark in business activities. 3. Jiang Haixin claimed that he had registered the domain name philipscis.com on search engines, and that this registration made the domain name widely known. In fact, search engines only provide websites or web pages containing certain keywords when Internet users enter those keywords; they do not automatically publicize registered content without user input. Merely registering on a search engine does not make a domain name widely known. On the contrary, only when Internet users want to learn about the defendant Philips or its trademark PHILIPS will they enter "PHILIPS" as a keyword, and then the search engine will provide domain names related to PHILIPS (including Jiang Haixin's registered philipscis.com domain name) to Internet users. Therefore, registering the domain name philipscis.com on search engines does not make it widely known; it only creates a misunderstanding among Internet users that the website corresponding to this domain name has some connection with Philips. Jiang Haixin has no rights or interests in the main part of the domain name and has no justifiable reasons for registering and using it.

Regarding the fourth issue: 1. After the PHILIPS trademark was registered in China in 1980, through the efforts of the defendant Philips, the trademark has gained considerable visibility in China. The first seven letters of the domain name registered by the plaintiff Jiang Haixin are completely identical to the PHILIPS trademark, and although the last three letters differ in order from the abbreviation CSI of Philips's department, the website corresponding to the disputed domain name primarily sells products from Philips's CSI department. 2. On the homepage of the website corresponding to the disputed domain name, not only did Philips's promotional slogan appear, but the letters "CSI" appeared in multiple places. Considering the domain name registered by Jiang Haixin and his use of it, it should be found that Jiang Haixin registered this domain name with the intention of exploiting Philips's visibility to mislead and attract Internet users to visit his website opened under this domain name, demonstrating malicious intent to infringe upon Philips's legitimate rights and interests.

In summary, the registration and use of the domain name philipscis.com by the plaintiff Jiang Haixin indeed infringed upon the defendant Philips's trademark rights. The WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center's decision to transfer the domain name philipscis.com to Philips was not improper. Therefore, Jiang Haixin's claim that he did not infringe Philips's rights and that the disputed domain name should belong to him was not supported.

Accordingly, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on December 25, 2003:

The claims of the plaintiff Jiang Haixin are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 1,000 shall be borne by the plaintiff Jiang Haixin.

After the judgment of first instance was rendered, neither party appealed, and the judgment of first instance became legally effective.
